title: Not a routine (Avot 2:13)
hookLine: don't make your prayer a fixed routine but a plea for mercy

lines: THE SAME WORDS, THREE TIMES A DAY.
cards: Love you, bye. You've said it at the end of a call so fast it came out as one word. Loveyoubye.
You meant it, sort of, but your mind was already on the next thing. Anything said every day can wear smooth like that, like a stone in a river.

Traditional Jewish prayer is said three times a day, mostly from a fixed prayer book. So the rabbis faced a real problem: how do you say the same words thousands of times without them turning into loveyoubye?
Rabbi Shimon, the fourth of the five students, has an answer.

teach.b: Rabbi Shimon says: be careful with the Shema and with prayer. When you pray, don't make your prayer keva, fixed, but a plea for mercy before God.
Then he gives a verse from the prophet Joel: God is gracious and full of compassion, slow to anger.

teach.h: REND YOUR HEART, NOT YOUR GARMENTS.
teach.b: The same verse begins, in the JPS translation, "rend your heart, and not your garments." Tear open your heart, not just your clothes. The outward sign isn't enough.
The Talmud stops to ask what keva actually means, and gives several answers. One sage says: prayer that feels like a burden, a chore to get through.
Others say: prayer that isn't said as a real request, the way a person actually pleads. Another says: prayer where you can't add anything new.
One rabbi admitted he could add something new, but was afraid he'd lose his place in the prayers. A very human moment. Here's the interesting part: nobody says throw out the prayer book.
The fixed words stay. They let a whole community pray together, with shared words, at shared times.
Rabbi Shimon asks only that the fixed words not make you fixed.
The Hebrew word for that inner attention is kavanah: intention, direction, aiming the heart. The words are the same.
You're the one who arrives new. He ends with one more line: don't be wicked in your own eyes. Don't give up on yourself.
Some commentators explain that someone who writes himself off stops trying to turn back.

how: Jewish prayer follows fixed texts in the siddur, said three times a day, and the tradition asks for kavanah, inner intention, and makes room for personal requests in one's own words within the Amidah.

o: a joyful song sung at a wedding feast
a printed prayer book, as opposed to free prayer
fixed, routine, said without the heart in it

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: don't be wicked in your own eyes

s: Rabbi Shimon says to stop using fixed prayers
the fixed words stay. he asks that they not become routine.
the Talmud gives several meanings of keva
a burden, not a real plea, or prayer where you can't add anything new.
one rabbi admitted he was afraid to add new words
he feared he would lose his place in the prayers.

games.q: you've said the same prayer every morning for years, and today the words feel empty. what does Rabbi Shimon suggest?
o: stop saying it until you feel it again.
keep the words, and fill them with real asking.
say it faster to get it done.
games.why: don't make your prayer keva, fixed, but a plea for mercy. the words stay the same; you arrive new.

practice: Pick words you say every day on autopilot, a blessing, a greeting, a goodnight, love you, bye, and say them silently, very slowly, meaning every word, as if for the first time.
If you pray, add one sentence of your own words to a prayer you already know; if you don't, just let one honest sentence of what you need rise up.

wordCard.voice: Keva. Fixed, routine: the word in Rabbi Shimon's warning not to let prayer become it, but a real plea from the heart, with kavanah.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: don't make your prayer fixed.

carryVoice: Your line: not rote. The same words, with a new heart each time. See you tomorrow.
